lesson.grammar_point: relative clauses with who, which, that and where

listenings.text: When I joined this group I was given an organisation chart with about two hundred names on it, and it was completely useless. Not wrong, just useless. It tells you who reports to whom, and that is almost never the question you have. The question you have is who is the person who actually knows how this gets approved. It took me a year to build the second map, the one that is not written down anywhere, and it looks nothing like the first. There is a woman in the legal division who has been there nineteen years and who can answer in four minutes a question that takes the official channel three weeks. There is an analyst in the region where most of our volume sits who knows every distributor personally. My advice to anybody joining a company this size is to stop reading the chart and start asking one question in every conversation: who is the person to talk to about this? Ask it fifty times and you will have something the chart cannot give you.

People ask me what makes a wine region, and they expect me to say the grape. It is almost never the grape. It is the place, and mostly it is the soil and what happens at night. Take a valley where the days are hot and the nights are cold. That difference is what keeps the acidity in the fruit, and acidity is what makes a wine that you can still drink with food twenty years later. Now take the same grape variety and plant it on a flat, warm plain, and you get something completely different and usually less interesting. This is why a region that nobody has heard of can be more exciting than a famous one. The famous names were mostly decided in the nineteenth century by whoever had a river to move barrels down. The interesting places today are the ones which have the right soil, the right nights and no reputation yet, and which are still run by families who cannot afford to make a wine that tastes like everybody else's.

paras: Anybody who has joined a large company has had the same experience. On the first day you are given a chart with two hundred names on it, and within a month you discover that it answers a question nobody actually asks. The chart tells you who reports to whom. What you need to know is who is the person who can answer this in four minutes instead of three weeks, which region is the one where most of the volume sits, and which colleague is the one everybody quietly calls before a decision goes up. That second map is never written down, and building it is most of what the first year in a big organisation really consists of.

Describing that map to somebody else is a language problem before it is anything else, because every useful sentence in it has the same shape. The analyst who handles the south. The division which was created two years ago. The region where the volume sits. A short clause hangs off a noun and tells you which one is meant, and without it you are left with names and titles that carry no information. It is the difference between saying that Ana is a specialist and saying that Ana is the specialist who has been in the legal division for nineteen years and who can approve this without going upstairs.

The same shape does something else, and it is not a coincidence. Ask anybody who knows about wine what makes a region, and the answer comes out in exactly this form: a valley where the days are hot and the nights are cold, a soil which holds water badly, families who cannot afford to make a wine that tastes like everybody else's. Places and people are described in the same way because in both cases the point is the same: not the name, but which one, and why that matters. Learn the structure once and you can introduce a colleague, explain a company, or describe a vineyard, without ever sounding like a list.
